title: Homeowner may be unaware of the scope of registration and device-enrollment data processing
description: During account registration and camera/sensor enrollment, the Home Hub may collect identifiers, device metadata, network details, and account information without making the homeowner sufficiently aware of what data is collected, for what purposes, how long it is stored, and whether it is disclosed onward. This creates a risk that the data subject is unaware of processing affecting their personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment flow includes collection of personal data and device-associated metadata, and that transparency notices or just-in-time explanations may be absent or insufficient.

title: Registration and enrollment may rely on invalid or insufficient consent
description: If the Home Hub collects or processes personal data from the homeowner during account creation and device enrollment without obtaining valid, specific, informed, and freely given consent where consent is the legal basis, the processing may be non-compliant. This is especially relevant if enrollment bundles optional analytics, diagnostics, or sharing into a single acceptance step.
assumptions: Assumes consent is used or presented as a legal basis for at least part of the processing, particularly optional processing beyond strict service necessity.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the actual legal basis and jurisdiction; if processing is instead based on contract or legitimate interest for strictly necessary functions, this node may only apply to optional processing.

title: Home Hub may collect unnecessary data types during account and device enrollment
description: The registration and enrollment flow may request or ingest more personal data than is strictly necessary to create the account and pair cameras/sensors, such as excessive profile details, precise location, contact data, or rich device/network metadata. Collecting unnecessary data types increases privacy exposure without functional need.
assumptions: Assumes the enrollment design could request optional or excessive fields beyond what is needed for authentication, ownership verification, and device pairing.

title: Enrollment data may be unnecessarily analyzed or enriched beyond setup needs
description: Data provided during registration and device enrollment may be further analyzed, correlated, or enriched—for example profiling the household based on enrolled device types, locations, or usage-related metadata—without necessity for basic account setup and pairing. Such unnecessary treatment expands disclosure risk through additional inferences.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub or connected services perform enrichment, profiling, or secondary analysis on enrollment data rather than limiting processing to setup functionality.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved context supports unnecessary processing generally, but whether enrichment actually occurs in this specific flow is not explicit.

title: Guest code entry can become attributable evidence of a specific guest action
description: If the Home Hub logs the temporary access code submission together with time, door, hub identity, or guest-related metadata, the event can serve as evidence that a particular guest attempted or performed an unlock action. This creates a non-repudiation privacy threat because the guest may be unable to plausibly deny the action later.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or forwards audit/event logs that bind the temporary code use to a guest, invitation, phone number, or other guest-associated record.

title: Temporary access code or associated metadata may identify the guest
description: Even if the flow only carries a temporary access code, the code may be unique per guest or per invitation. When processed by the Home Hub, that code can act as an identifier, directly or indirectly revealing which guest is at the door at a given time.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are uniquely assigned or resolvable by the system to a specific guest, booking, or invitation.

title: Repeated guest access events may enable profiling of an individual's visit patterns
description: If the Home Hub records repeated uses of temporary codes over time, those events can be linked to build a profile of a guest's arrival times, frequency of visits, and behavioral patterns. This goes beyond a single unlock event and creates a linking/profiling privacy threat.
assumptions: Assumes access events are retained and linkable across sessions via the same guest identity, invitation, code family, or correlated metadata.

title: Guest may be unaware that entering the temporary code shares personal data
description: A guest may perceive code entry as a simple door-unlock action, while the Home Hub may also collect personal data such as the fact of presence at the property, timestamp of arrival, and association with a specific invitation or identity. If this collection is not made clear, the guest is unaware of personal-data sharing.
assumptions: Assumes the interface does not clearly inform the guest about what data is collected, how long it is retained, or who can access it.

title: Sensitive in-home activity events exposed through local log access
description: The local event log stores motion, door, and sensor events that reveal occupancy patterns, routines, and behavior inside the home. If the datastore is accessible to additional local users, apps, maintenance interfaces, or other anticipated parties beyond what is necessary, these personal data become excessively exposed.
assumptions: The event log contains timestamped household activity data and may be readable by components or users other than the minimum necessary writer/reader set.

title: No user preference or consent control over logging of household events
description: Home Hub writes sensor events into the local event log, but the data subject may lack any way to configure whether such events are logged, which event categories are stored, or how long they remain stored. This creates a lack of control over collection and storage preferences for personal data.
assumptions: Residents or visitors are data subjects for the logged events, and the system may not provide granular logging preferences or consent controls.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the product lacks configurable logging preferences or consent controls; the flow alone does not prove whether such controls exist.

title: Cloud clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub to cloud video storage may be stored indefinitely or beyond the stated purpose/retention period, creating a violation of the storage limitation principle for personal data contained in the videos.
assumptions: The uploaded clips contain personal data such as identifiable occupants, visitors, or bystanders, and DS2 is responsible for enforcing retention/deletion.

title: Data subjects may be unaware that camera clips are uploaded to the cloud
description: Occupants, visitors, or bystanders captured in recorded clips may not be aware that footage is transferred from the Home Hub to cloud video storage for remote retention and further processing.
assumptions: The system records identifiable individuals and does not provide sufficiently clear notice at the point of collection/upload.

title: Users may lack effective preferences or consent controls for cloud upload
description: The Home Hub may upload recorded clips to cloud storage without giving the user granular preferences or consent options to disable upload, limit which cameras/clips are uploaded, or choose retention behavior, reducing intervenability over processing.
assumptions: Cloud upload is enabled by default or controls are incomplete or hard to exercise.

title: Improper management of uploaded video as personal data
description: Cloud video storage may process uploaded clips without adequate personal-data management practices, such as incomplete deletion propagation, poor metadata handling, or inadequate lifecycle management, leading to privacy harms beyond pure security concerns.
assumptions: DS2 stores both video content and associated metadata and may replicate or back up data across storage tiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Nc.2 is broad in the retrieved context; this mapping is plausible but less specific than Nc.1.1.4.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware cybersecurity risk management for stored clips
description: Cloud storage of recorded camera clips may lack risk management measures that account for the privacy sensitivity of video data, increasing the chance that operational or security weaknesses translate into privacy violations affecting recorded individuals.
assumptions: Video clips are sensitive personal data and DS2's controls may not be tailored to privacy impact.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 is applicable at a governance level, but the exact fit to this single flow is somewhat approximate.

title: Motion alerts may be exposed to more backend parties than necessary
description: The real-time motion alert forwarded from the Home Hub to the mobile app backend contains occupancy-related personal data. If the backend distributes, stores, or makes this alert accessible to internal services, operators, or third parties beyond what is necessary to deliver the notification, the data is excessively exposed.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert can reveal behavior or presence patterns of household occupants and that the backend may involve multiple downstream recipients or support personnel.

title: Backend may unnecessarily enrich or analyze motion alerts
description: Once the motion alert reaches the mobile app backend, it may be further analyzed, correlated with other household events, or enriched into behavioral profiles beyond what is needed to notify the user. Such secondary treatment increases privacy exposure.
assumptions: Assumes the backend performs analytics, profiling, or retention-linked processing in addition to simple message relay.

title: Users may lack control over forwarding and processing of motion alerts
description: Household occupants or account holders may be unable to choose whether motion alerts are forwarded to the backend, which recipients receive them, or how long they are retained and processed there. This reduces data subject control over occupancy-related personal data.
assumptions: Assumes configuration options for disabling cloud forwarding, limiting recipients, or setting retention are absent or insufficient.

title: Occupants may be unaware that motion events are shared with the backend
description: People in the home may not realize that a detected motion event is transmitted off the device to the mobile app backend in real time. This is especially relevant for non-account-holder occupants or visitors whose activity triggers the alert.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform all affected individuals that motion detections are sent to cloud/backend infrastructure.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware security controls for motion-alert transmission
description: If the transmission and backend handling of real-time motion alerts are not covered by adequate cybersecurity risk management, privacy risks such as unauthorized access, overcollection, or insecure onward sharing may not be properly mitigated. This creates a non-compliance risk where privacy and security controls are insufficiently integrated.
assumptions: Assumes missing or weak risk assessment and governance around this alert flow rather than a specific technical flaw visible from the DFD alone.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance-level inference from the flow and context rather than a directly evidenced property of the depicted data flow.

title: Excessive detail in motion notification discloses personal data
description: If the backend includes unnecessary details in the push notification content (e.g., exact time patterns, room/camera location, thumbnails, or rich contextual text), personal data about occupancy and behavior may be disclosed beyond what is necessary to alert the homeowner. Such content can also become visible on lock screens or notification previews on the recipient device.
assumptions: Assumes the notification may contain more than a minimal alert and that device notification previews may be enabled.
uncertainty_note: Dd.3.1 is primarily about unnecessary treatment/enrichment; I am applying it here to unnecessary disclosure in notification payload/content, which is a close but not perfect fit.

title: Homeowner may lack preference controls over motion notification content and delivery
description: The homeowner may be unable to control whether motion events are pushed at all, what level of detail is shown, or whether sensitive content appears on the phone screen. This reduces the data subject's ability to set privacy-preserving preferences for processing and disclosure of personal data through notifications.
assumptions: Assumes the system offers limited or no settings for notification granularity, preview visibility, or opt-in/opt-out behavior.
uncertainty_note: This depends on product design; if robust notification/privacy settings exist, this threat may not apply.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware risk management for push-notification channel
description: If the backend sends motion-detected notifications without adequately assessing privacy risks of the push-notification channel—such as exposure on lock screens, third-party push infrastructure, or over-detailed payloads—the system may fail to manage cybersecurity and privacy risks in a compliant manner.
assumptions: Assumes privacy risks specific to mobile push notifications were not fully assessed or mitigated during design and operation.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on applicable legal/policy obligations and actual governance practices, which are not provided in the flow description.

title: Disclosure of analytics data to a predetermined third-party vendor
description: The mobile app backend shares aggregated device-usage analytics with a cloud analytics vendor, creating a data disclosure threat because personal data or data relating to users/devices is transferred to a fixed external party. Even if described as aggregated, the dataset may still reveal information about groups or become personal data when combined with other data held by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes EE3 is a known, fixed analytics provider rather than a dynamically changing recipient set, and that the shared analytics concerns user/device behavior that may still qualify as personal data or privacy-relevant data.

title: Aggregated analytics may still contain pseudonymous device-level identifiers
description: If the backend includes persistent device, installation, account, or session identifiers in the analytics payload, the vendor could distinguish or single out users/devices even without direct real-world names. This makes data subjects identifiable through pseudonymous references.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics is not fully anonymized and may include stable identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or small-cell aggregates that permit singling out.
uncertainty_note: The flow description says 'aggregated device-usage analytics', so direct pseudonyms may be absent; this threat applies if aggregation still preserves stable device/app-instance references or sufficiently granular segments.

title: Insufficient privacy and cybersecurity risk management for third-party analytics sharing
description: Sharing analytics with an external cloud vendor can create non-compliance risk if the controller has not adequately assessed privacy and cybersecurity risks, defined roles and responsibilities, ensured lawful basis and transparency, and imposed appropriate contractual and technical safeguards for the transfer.
assumptions: Assumes the organization may rely on the vendor for analytics processing and that compliance obligations apply to this transfer, such as vendor due diligence, data processing terms, transfer assessment, retention limits, and purpose limitation.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance/compliance threat inferred from the existence of third-party sharing; applicability depends on whether appropriate assessments, notices, contracts, and safeguards are already in place.

title: Homeowner may be unaware that stored video is retrieved and processed for playback
description: When the backend retrieves a stored video clip from cloud storage to serve playback, the data subject or user may not be sufficiently informed that their video is being accessed, processed, and transmitted at playback time, including any associated metadata handling.
assumptions: Applies if the system does not clearly inform users about playback-time retrieval/processing in notices or UI.
uncertainty_note: Retrieved context directly supports U.1.1, but applicability depends on whether transparency about playback retrieval is already provided.

title: User may lack control over preferences for retrieval and playback processing of stored video
description: The backend's retrieval of stored clips for playback may occur without giving the homeowner meaningful control over relevant privacy preferences, such as whether clips remain available for remote playback, whether certain clips can be hidden or restricted, or whether playback-related processing is enabled.
assumptions: Applies if the product offers insufficient privacy controls over storage/playback availability or related processing.
uncertainty_note: Retrieved context supports U.2.1, but the exact preference controls expected are product-specific.

title: Stored video may be retained longer than necessary before backend retrieval
description: Because the backend retrieves clips from cloud storage for playback, there is a risk that personal video data remains stored and retrievable beyond the period necessary for the stated purpose, violating storage limitation expectations.
assumptions: Applies if retention periods are not enforced or clips remain accessible indefinitely in cloud storage.
uncertainty_note: Retrieved context directly supports storage limitation, though this is primarily a datastore retention issue manifested in this retrieval flow.

title: Backend retrieval path may lack privacy-aware cybersecurity risk management
description: The retrieval of stored video from cloud storage to the backend creates a privacy-relevant attack surface. If privacy risks are not considered in cybersecurity risk management for this retrieval path, personal video content and metadata may be exposed or mishandled in ways that lead to non-compliance.
assumptions: Applies if threat modeling, access control review, logging minimization, or secure transfer controls for this retrieval path are insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Retrieved context supports Nc.3 at a general level; exact control gaps are not specified in the flow description.
